title: Born With 0 Freckles. Why Do Some People Get Hundreds?
description:
Why do some people get way more freckles than others? See how sunlight switches on the pigment cells in your skin, why freckles fade in winter, how the MC1R gene links freckles to red hair, and how a freckle differs from a sun spot.

topic: Why do some people get way more freckles than others?
script: You were born with zero freckles. Not a single one. They usually start showing up around age two. Then some kids get a few, while others end up with hundreds. So why do some people get way more freckles than others? First, what is a freckle, really? Your skin gets its color from a pigment called melanin. It's made by special cells called melanocytes, tucked deep in the bottom layer of your skin. Each one pumps out tiny packets of pigment, and hands them to the skin cells around it. Here's the surprise. A freckle doesn't have extra pigment cells. It has about the same number as the skin next to it. Those cells are just working way harder, making a lot more melanin in one tiny spot. Most freckles are smaller than three millimeters. And they show up most on fair skin, which has less melanin to begin with. So what makes those cells work overtime? Sunlight. When ultraviolet light hits your skin, it switches your melanocytes into high gear. Melanin is your body's sunshade. It soaks up UV light before it can damage your DNA. In most skin, that extra melanin spreads out evenly, and you get a tan. But in freckly skin, it piles up in little patches. That's why freckles darken every summer, and fade, or even disappear, in winter. And it's why babies, who've barely seen the sun, don't have any yet. But two kids can play in the same sun, and only one ends up covered in freckles. That's where your genes come in. The big one is a gene called MC1R. Think of it as a switch on every melanocyte. When it works normally, the cell makes eumelanin, a dark brown pigment that's great at blocking sun. But scientists have found more than 80 versions of MC1R. And some of them are ancient. One may date back around 80,000 years. Some of them flip the switch toward pheomelanin instead, a reddish yellow pigment that protects much less. Those same versions are behind red hair. Most redheads carry two of them, and almost all carry at least one. That's why red hair and freckles so often go together. Still, one copy doesn't guarantee freckles. Some people without these versions freckle anyway, because lots of other genes play a part too. Now, not every brown spot is a freckle. Doctors call real freckles ephelides. Real freckles come and go with the seasons, and many fade as you get older. Sun spots, or solar lentigines, are different. They're larger, they show up in middle age, after years of sun, and they stay put all winter long. Under a microscope, sun spots really do have extra pigment cells. So what do freckles tell you? Freckly skin usually makes less of that protective brown melanin, so it burns more easily. That's why skin doctors tell freckly people, to be extra careful with sunscreen. So freckles aren't random dots. They're tiny patches of sunshade, switched on extra hard, mostly thanks to one tiny gene. Next up, how do your lungs breathe, more than 20,000 times a day?
key_facts: Freckles are rare on infants and commonly first appear around age 2 (Medscape)
Freckles have about the same number of melanocytes as nearby skin; the cells make more melanin (Wikipedia, DermNet, Medscape)
UV light increases melanin production; freckles darken in summer and fade in winter (DermNet)
Ephelides are usually under 3 mm across (DermNet)
More than 80 MC1R variants have been identified (Helix); some MC1R variants linked to freckling and red hair, one (Arg160Trp) estimated ~80,000 years old (Wikipedia)
Most redheads have two MC1R variants and almost all have one (Wikipedia)
Solar lentigines are larger, appear in middle age, persist in winter and have more melanocytes (DermNet, Medscape)
Freckly skin has less photo-protective melanin and is more susceptible to UV damage (Wikipedia)
